title: Four US trawl samples gave no clear sea temperature link to catch latitude spread in 1982-2019
abstract: We tested whether annual sea surface temperature changes had a link to the north-south spread of catch biomass. We used fixed survey strata and persistent taxa in the Bering Sea and Northeast US fall surveys in 1982-1999 and 2000-2019. Models controlled changes in a regional biomass index. Temperature slopes were +2.94, -0.92, +2.61 and -2.76 km per C. All four adjusted bootstrap intervals included zero. Planned changes to the temperature window, biomass adjustment, regional summary and block length also gave intervals across zero. These results do not establish expansion, contraction or a small effect. Selected taxa, fixed survey boundaries, surface rather than bottom temperature, short records and residual observation bias limit inference. The package gives code, sufficient catch evidence, monthly temperature data, uncertainty estimates, source hashes and reproduction instructions.

display.caption: Annual change in catch latitude standard deviation per 1 C annual SST change. Models control a biomass index. Bars are approximate 98.75% marginal bootstrap intervals for four main tests. All include zero.

citations.reason: Verified monthly regional SST series and source provenance. Underlying catch observations overlap. Our outcome is latitude spread, not the prior centroid timing contrast.
Prior survey-effort comparison motivates fixed strata and area weights.
